goals: Isolate the mechanistic effect of soil clay content on runoff vs recharge partitioning
key_processes: Infiltration capacity as a function of soil texture
Hydraulic conductivity control on subsurface drainage
Surface runoff generation when infiltration capacity is exceeded

model_choice.rationale: Single-column ELM represents soil texture effects on infiltration, runoff (QOVER), and subsurface drainage (QDRAI) as core physics. A controlled experiment with synthetic uniform soils isolates the clay-content effect without confounding spatial heterogeneity.

answerable: Soil texture control on infiltration and runoff/recharge partitioning via ELM's Richards equation and hydraulic conductivity parameterizations
Quantitative partitioning response across the clay content range (5-55%) under controlled forcing

sampling_strategy.approach: controlled factor levels (treatments), not spatial sampling
sampling_strategy.n_justification: Six clay levels span the 5-55% range with sufficient resolution to capture the nonlinear hydraulic response (sandy to clayey soils). Each level is one treatment; no replication needed in a deterministic model under fixed forcing.
sampling_strategy.placement_logic: Not applicable — this is a controlled experiment in parameter space, not geographic space. All columns use the same arbitrary location and forcing.

sampling_plan.reason: Sandy soil (5% clay): high infiltration capacity, minimal surface runoff, maximum recharge
Loamy sand (15% clay): moderate infiltration, beginning of runoff generation under intense precipitation
Loam (25% clay): balanced infiltration and runoff, mid-range recharge
Clay loam (35% clay): reduced infiltration, increased surface runoff, declining recharge
Silty clay (45% clay): low infiltration capacity, high runoff generation, minimal recharge
Clay (55% clay): lowest infiltration, maximum surface runoff, near-zero recharge

validation_design.observation_source: None — conceptual experiment validated against physical expectation and literature (e.g., Rawls & Brakensiek infiltration curves, Clapp & Hornberger hydraulic parameters)
validation_design.comparison: Process validation: monotonic decrease in infiltration and recharge with increasing clay content; comparison to published soil hydraulic property databases
validation_design.metric: Qualitative consistency with expected infiltration-texture relationships; quantitative comparison of QOVER/QDRAI ratios to literature ranges

experiment_summary.primary_treatment: 15-year simulation (10 years spin-up + 5 years analysis) with representative forcing period (e.g., 1990-2004), uniform vegetation (generic temperate PFT), synthetic uniform soil columns with specified clay content, fixed location/elevation

requires_capabilities.why: Recharge (QDRAI) is a target variable. Without spin-up, the aquifer cold-starts at default WTD (~8.8 m) and QDRAI reads near-zero while storage fills — an initialization artifact, not the soil-texture effect. Spin-up is needed to equilibrate the aquifer and produce meaningful recharge values.
requires_capabilities.blocks: Meaningful recharge output and runoff/recharge partitioning analysis

requires_capabilities.why: The experiment requires uniform soil columns with specified clay percentages (5%, 15%, 25%, 35%, 45%, 55%), overriding default SSURGO data. ELM likely supports custom soil parameters via namelist or fsurdat modification, but this must be confirmed.
requires_capabilities.blocks: Creation of the controlled soil treatments

requires_capabilities.capability: Runoff and recharge output variables (QOVER, QDRAI)
requires_capabilities.why: The experiment targets runoff/recharge partitioning. QOVER (surface runoff) and QDRAI (subsurface drainage/recharge) must be in the history output. These are standard ELM variables, but explicit confirmation is needed.

assumptions: ELM's soil hydraulic parameterizations (e.g., Clapp & Hornberger or van Genuchten) adequately represent the clay-content effect on infiltration and drainage across the 5-55% range
A 10-year spin-up is sufficient to equilibrate the aquifer for recharge analysis (may need verification for clayey soils with very slow drainage)
Vegetation and forcing are held constant across treatments, so observed partitioning differences are attributable to soil texture alone
The chosen forcing period (e.g., 1990-2004) is climatically representative and includes sufficient precipitation variability to exercise the infiltration-runoff mechanism
No lateral flow or regional groundwater effects are needed — single-column 1-D representation is adequate for this controlled experiment
open_questions: What forcing period (within 1980-2018) should be used? A wetter period may better differentiate runoff generation across clay levels.
Should sand and silt percentages be held constant (e.g., fixed sand/silt ratio) or varied to maintain realistic soil texture triangles for each clay level?
Is 10 years of spin-up sufficient for the clayey end (55% clay) where drainage is very slow, or should spin-up be extended?
Should the experiment include a sensitivity check on forcing intensity (e.g., repeat with a wet vs dry 5-year period) to test if the clay effect is modulated by climate?
